docs.title: kind: Entity — fuse
docs.text:
Fuse N legacy tables into one canonical, queryable thing. Each source keeps landing in its own table; the manifest says how their columns map onto one shape and which column identifies the same real-world row across systems. The hub compiles that into a SQL view — and every disagreement between sources is kept in a _conflicts ledger on the row, never silently resolved.

Kind Entity Compiles to connector.v_<name> — a view; each tenant sees only its own rows Sources any table in the connector schema: a CSV, JDBC or Kafka connector's t_* Lookups optional joins[] — a table that enriches the fused rows without adding one Apply lm entity apply — lm_admin; validate-then-compile, atomic Read lm entity get NAME — lm_user, scope-bound; also lm view, lm ask Edition Open

The ERP has a customer table, the CRM has another. An entity declares which one wins, exposes one row per customer, and records per row and per column where the systems disagree.

That ledger is what a kind: View shows under Ambiguïtés et divergences, and what lm conflicts list lists across every entity you can read.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Join without collapsing. A lookup table enriches each fused row — one row per product with its category — and an ambiguous lookup key is shown, never guessed.
  • Priority is the source order, per column. The first source that has a value wins that column; a source that has none lets the next one fill the gap, which is never a conflict.
  • Nothing is dropped. Two distinct non-null values for one column land in the row's _conflicts ledger with the source that said each.
  • Grounding for the surfaces above. Labels a view renders, descriptions the chat reads, and a values domain the filters enforce — refusing what is outside it rather than returning an empty table.
  • Askable immediately. Applying an entity rediscovers its scopes' schema cards; the fused view is in the chat's vocabulary before the next question.
  • Refused before compiled. A manifest that cannot compile is not saved, and every refusal is a 400 that says exactly what to change.
  • The delete interlock. A connector whose table feeds an entity cannot be deleted until the entity is — a 409 that names both.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
Every screen on this page reads the demo desk that ships with the repo

Two customer exports that disagree and an order book, under docs/apps/demo/. Three commands land them; the hand count of what the fusion must give is on The demo desk.

# 10-customer.yaml — one Customer fused from the ERP and the CRM on the customer code.
#
# The ERP is listed first, so on a disagreement its value is the representative and the
# CRM's is kept in the row's _conflicts ledger — nothing is silently dropped. The `columns`
# block grounds the canonical shape for the surfaces above: labels a kind:View renders,
# descriptions the chat reads, and a `values` domain the filters enforce.
#
# Expect: 14 rows (12 ERP + 2 CRM-only; the CRM's blank-code row is excluded), and exactly
#         three in dispute — P-1000 (name), P-1002 (city), P-1008 (city). P-1005 is not one:
#         the ERP had no city and the CRM filled it, and a gap is not a disagreement.
kind: Entity
name: AcmeCustomer
description: "A customer, fused from the ERP export and the CRM export."
match: [code]
scopes: [desk]
columns:
  code:
    label: "Code client"
  name:
    label: "Raison sociale"
  city:
    label: "Ville"
    description: "Billing city, free text."
    example: "Lyon"
  segment:
    label: "Segment"
    description: "Commercial segment."
    values: [GOLD, SILVER, BRONZE]
  credit_limit:
    label: "Encours autorisé"
    description: "Credit limit in euros."
  email:
    label: "Email"
sources:
  - table: t_acme_desk_erp
    map:
      code: code
      name: name
      city: city
      segment: segment
      credit_limit: credit_limit
  - table: t_acme_desk_crm
    map:
      customer: code
      company: name
      town: city
      email: email

$ lm entity apply -f docs/apps/demo/entities/10-customer.yaml
Applied entity "AcmeCustomer" → connector."v_acmecustomer"

There is no lm entity validate: apply refuses a manifest that would not compile, before anything is written. Read the result with lm entity get (name lower-cased, --filter an exact match on a canonical column):

$ lm entity get acmecustomer --filter city=Lyon -o json
[
  {
    "code": "P-1000",
    "name": "Hydraulique Lyon 1000",
    "city": "Lyon",
    "segment": "GOLD",
    "credit_limit": "500",
    "email": "contact@hydraulique-lyon.example",
    "_conflicts": "{\"name\": [{\"src\": \"t_acme_desk_erp\", \"value\": \"Hydraulique Lyon 1000\"}, {\"src\": \"t_acme_desk_crm\", \"value\": \"HYDRAULIQUE LYON\"}]}"
  },
  {
    "code": "P-1008",
    "name": "Filtration Lyon 1008",
    "city": "Lyon",
    "segment": "GOLD",
    "credit_limit": "1596",
    "email": "contact@filtration-lyon.example",
    "_conflicts": "{\"city\": [{\"src\": \"t_acme_desk_erp\", \"value\": \"Lyon\"}, {\"src\": \"t_acme_desk_crm\", \"value\": \"Villeurbanne\"}]}"
  }
]

Two customers in Lyon, and on each the CRM disagrees with the ERP. The ERP is first in sources[], so its value is in the column; the CRM's is in the ledger.

Fourteen rows in all: twelve from the ERP, two the CRM alone knows. The CRM's row with no customer code is absent: a NULL match key matches nothing.

Where the systems disagree, across every entity at once:

$ lm conflicts list
ENTITY        KEY     COLUMNS  SOURCES
AcmeCustomer  P-1000  name     t_acme_desk_erp,t_acme_desk_crm
AcmeCustomer  P-1002  city     t_acme_desk_erp,t_acme_desk_crm
AcmeCustomer  P-1008  city     t_acme_desk_erp,t_acme_desk_crm

Three rows in dispute, exactly the three the hand count predicted. P-1005 is not one of them: the ERP had no city for it, the CRM did, and the fused row simply carries Aarhus.

docs.title: The manifest
Fusion semantics
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  s1[("t_acme_desk_erp<br/>P-1000 · name: Hydraulique Lyon 1000")] --> f
  s2[("t_acme_desk_crm<br/>P-1000 · company: HYDRAULIQUE LYON")] --> f
  f["fusion — union of all sources,<br/>grouped by the match column"] --> c[("v_acmecustomer<br/>P-1000 · name: Hydraulique Lyon 1000<br/>first non-null, source order")]
  f -.-> k["_conflicts<br/>name: Hydraulique Lyon 1000 ↔ HYDRAULIQUE LYON<br/>nothing silently dropped"]

The compiled view unions every source and groups by the match column(s):

  • a source row whose match column is NULL is excluded — it cannot be matched to anything;
  • for every other column, the representative is the first non-null by source order. The choice is made per column, independently: a source that wins name has no claim on city;
  • a NULL is not an opinion: a source with no value lets the next one fill the gap, and that is never recorded as a conflict. Only two or more distinct non-null values are;
  • when sources genuinely disagree, the representative still follows source order, and all the values land in the _conflicts ledger;
  • a column may name the source that goes first for it alone — prefer: in its columns: entry. The others keep the declared order.

Flip the order and nothing but the representatives changes. 20-crm-first.yaml lists the CRM first over the same two tables:

$ lm entity apply -f docs/apps/demo/entities/20-crm-first.yaml
Applied entity "AcmeCustomerCrmFirst" → connector."v_acmecustomercrmfirst"
$ lm entity get acmecustomercrmfirst --filter code=P-1000 -o json
[
  {
    "code": "P-1000",
    "name": "HYDRAULIQUE LYON",
    "city": "Lyon",
    "email": "contact@hydraulique-lyon.example",
    "segment": "GOLD",
    "credit_limit": "500",
    "_conflicts": "{\"name\": [{\"src\": \"t_acme_desk_crm\", \"value\": \"HYDRAULIQUE LYON\"}, {\"src\": \"t_acme_desk_erp\", \"value\": \"Hydraulique Lyon 1000\"}]}"
  }
]

Same fourteen rows, same three disputes; P-1000 now reads HYDRAULIQUE LYON, and segment — which the CRM does not carry — still comes from the ERP. Each tenant sees only its own rows through the fusion.

docs.title: When a source row changes
docs.text:
Run the connector again after the source changed, and the entity shows the new value. On the demo desk, the ERP said Milano for P-1002 and the CRM said Milan — one of the three disputes above:

$ lm entity get acmecustomer --filter code=P-1002 -o json
[
  {
    "code": "P-1002",
    "name": "Fixations Milano 1002",
    "city": "Milano",
    "segment": "BRONZE",
    "credit_limit": "774",
    "email": "ventes@fixations-milano.example",
    "_conflicts": "{\"city\": [{\"src\": \"t_acme_desk_erp\", \"value\": \"Milano\"}, {\"src\": \"t_acme_desk_crm\", \"value\": \"Milan\"}]}"
  }
]

The ERP corrects its export to Milan. Put the new file in place and run the connector:

docker cp acme-erp.csv lumnik-hub-1:/tmp/acme-desk/acme-erp.csv
lm connector run acme-desk-erp

$ lm entity get acmecustomer --filter code=P-1002 -o json
[
  {
    "code": "P-1002",
    "name": "Fixations Milano 1002",
    "city": "Milan",
    "segment": "BRONZE",
    "credit_limit": "774",
    "email": "ventes@fixations-milano.example",
    "_conflicts": "{}"
  }
]
$ lm conflicts list
ENTITY                KEY     COLUMNS  SOURCES
AcmeCustomer          P-1000  name     t_acme_desk_erp,t_acme_desk_crm
AcmeCustomer          P-1008  city     t_acme_desk_erp,t_acme_desk_crm
AcmeCustomerCrmFirst  P-1000  name     t_acme_desk_crm,t_acme_desk_erp
AcmeCustomerCrmFirst  P-1008  city     t_acme_desk_crm,t_acme_desk_erp

The ERP's old value is gone from the row and from the ledger. The same holds for a joins[] lookup (a renamed category shows its new name) and for a resolution: entity. If one export lists the same customer twice with two different values, both stay in _conflicts.

The demo's ERP connector reads one local file, so each run is a full refresh. Remove P-1011 from the file and run again: the customer leaves the source table and the entity.

$ lm run get 630cee80
ID        CONNECTOR      ENDPOINT  STATUS     IN  OUT  SKIPPED  DEAD-LETTERS  STARTED           ENDED
630cee80  acme-desk-erp  default   Completed  11  11   0        0             2026-10-19 07:28  2026-10-19 07:28
• 1 row(s) removed — the source no longer holds them
$ lm entity get acmecustomer --filter code=P-1011
no rows

Put Milano back in the file and run again: the dispute with the CRM returns.

$ lm entity get acmecustomer --filter code=P-1002 -o json
[
  {
    "code": "P-1002",
    "name": "Fixations Milano 1002",
    "city": "Milano",
    "segment": "BRONZE",
    "credit_limit": "774",
    "email": "ventes@fixations-milano.example",
    "_conflicts": "{\"city\": [{\"src\": \"t_acme_desk_erp\", \"value\": \"Milano\"}, {\"src\": \"t_acme_desk_crm\", \"value\": \"Milan\"}]}"
  }
]

What happens to a row deleted at the source:

Source A row deleted at the source csv-file, one local file removed at the next run (above) csv-file drop folder, sftp, s3 stays — see CSV & files jdbc-generic stays — see Deletes are never propagated kafka stays — a tombstone goes to the dead letters, see Tombstones

docs.title: Dates across sources
docs.text:
The same business date does not land under the same type from every source:

Source Lands as 1 July 2026 reads an Oracle DATE, a PostgreSQL timestamp (no zone) a timestamp, its wall clock read in the connection's zone, UTC without one 2026-07-01 00:00:00+00 a PostgreSQL timestamptz, an Oracle TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE a timestamp, the instant 2026-07-01 00:00:00+00 a PostgreSQL date, a CSV column through parse-date with a date-only format a date 2026-07-01 a CSV column left as written, a Kafka field text 01/07/2026

The fused column follows what its sources hold:

  • every source a date → the entity's column is a date;
  • dates and timestamps mixed → a timestamp, a date being its midnight UTC. A source that only knows the day cannot contradict an hour, so the sources are compared at the day: an ERP's 2026-07-01 14:30 and a CSV's 2026-07-01 agree, a CSV's 2026-07-02 is a conflict. The timed sources among themselves still compare to the instant. The value shown is a time before a day, whatever the order of sources: a day never hides the hour beside it;
  • one source text → the column stays text, compared as written, as every other text column. The hub does not guess whether 01/07 is the first of July or the seventh of January.

A match: column follows the same rule: an ERP's 2026-07-01 00:00 and a CSV's 2026-07-01 are one record.

An ERP's due_at (a timestamp) fused with a partner CSV's due parsed as dd/MM/yyyy (a date), and both systems' shipped, which the CSV leaves as written:

$ lm source schema --scope livedesk
…
connector.v_liveorder
  order_no                 text
  due                      timestamp with time zone
  shipped                  text
  status                   text
$ lm entity get liveorder --filter due=2026-07-01 -o json
[
  {
    "order_no": "SO-1",
    "due": "2026-07-01T00:00:00Z",
    "shipped": "2026-07-03 14:30:00+00",
    "status": "open",
    "_conflicts": "{\"shipped\": [{\"src\": \"t_live_erp_orders\", \"value\": \"2026-07-03 14:30:00+00\"}, {\"src\": \"t_live_partner_orders\", \"value\": \"03/07/2026\"}]}"
  }
]

due agrees: the ERP's midnight and the CSV's day are one instant. shipped is text, and two writings of the same day are a conflict. To type it, the CSV's table must be created again: a table the hub created keeps its column types, and a new parse-date alone changes nothing.

  1. lm entity delete liveorder — the entity holds the table;
  2. lm connector delete live-partner-orders — drops its table and data;
  3. add - parse-date: { column: shipped, formats: ["dd/MM/yyyy"] } to its cell: hooks, lm apply it, and lm connector run it;
  4. lm entity apply the entity again: shipped is now timestamp with time zone.

Once typed, the CSV's 03/07/2026 and the ERP's 2026-07-03 14:30 agree: the same day.

A time of day has one more trap: the zone it was written in. An ERP's 2026-08-02 23:30 with no zone lands as 23:30 UTC unless its connection declares one. The same time in a CSV parsed with zone: Europe/Paris lands as 21:30 UTC: two hours apart, a conflict on every such row:

$ lm entity get liveorder --filter order_id=1 -o json
[
  {
    "order_id": "1",
    "ordered_at": "2026-08-02T23:30:00Z",
    "_conflicts": "{\"ordered_at\": [{\"src\": \"t_orders\", \"value\": \"2026-08-02 23:30:00+00\"}, {\"src\": \"t_partner\", \"value\": \"2026-08-02 21:30:00+00\"}]}"
  }
]

Declare where each source writes: zone: Europe/Paris under the ERP's connection, the same zone on the CSV's parse-date. Once the ERP's table is read again (the gesture), both hold the same instant:

$ lm entity get liveorder -o json
[
  {
    "order_id": "1",
    "ordered_at": "2026-08-02T21:30:00Z",
    "_conflicts": "{}"
  },
  {
    "order_id": "2",
    "ordered_at": "2026-01-15T22:30:00Z",
    "_conflicts": "{}"
  }
]

A date alone has no such trap: both sides are its midnight UTC.

A typed column is a date everywhere the entity is read: a view filters it as a date, lm ask sees its type, an entity read and an export write it in UTC whatever zone the hub runs in. The decision is taken at apply: an entity applied before a source changed type keeps its columns until it is applied again.

docs.title: Numbers across sources
docs.text:
A number lands as one when its source types it: a JDBC INTEGER or BIGINT (a bigint), a JDBC NUMERIC, DECIMAL or Oracle NUMBER (a decimal, 1000021.0000), a CSV column through parse-number (integer: true for a bigint) — when the chunk that creates the column holds a number; all empty there, it is created text. A CSV column left as written is text.

The fused column follows what its sources hold, as for dates:

  • every source a whole number → the entity's column is a bigint;
  • one decimal among them → a numeric, written without trailing zeros: an ERP's 7.0000 and a CSV's 7 are one value — one record when it is the match: key, no conflict otherwise, and 1500.0000 reads "1500";
  • one source text → the column stays text, compared as written: "10.0" and 10 disagree.

A number column then orders as a number — 7, 12, 100, never 100, 12, 7 — in an entity read, a View and an export, and = compares it by value: --filter amount=1500.00 finds 1500. It still reads as a string. An entity applied before its sources were typed keeps its text columns until it is applied again.

docs.title: The _conflicts ledger
docs.text:
One JSON object per row, one key per disputed column, {} — never null — when everyone agrees:

{
  "city": [
    { "src": "t_acme_desk_erp", "value": "Lyon" },
    { "src": "t_acme_desk_crm", "value": "Villeurbanne" }
  ]
}

Where it shows:

  • on every read of the entity (lm entity get);
  • at the foot of a record's detail in a kind: View;
  • across every entity in lm conflicts list — see Aggregated conflicts.

The chat cannot query it: "where do the ERP and the CRM disagree?" is a question for lm conflicts list, not lm ask. An lm ask answer that filtered on a disputed value names the record in a disputed block (Disputed rows).

docs.title: Fuse or join
docs.text:
Two different things happen between legacy tables, and an entity keeps them apart:

Identity fusion (match + sources[]) Relational enrichment (joins[]) The question several systems describe the same object one object references another Example the ERP's customer and the CRM's customer a product and its category Rows merged into one per match key the primary rows are never collapsed or multiplied Disagreement kept in _conflicts, first source wins the column none — a lookup is not an opinion

match: [category_id] is not enrichment: it would group every product of a category into one identity and turn their differing names into conflicts. To keep one row per product and bring the category's fields along, declare the category table as a lookup:

kind: Entity
name: ProductWithCategory
description: One row per product, enriched with its category — a join, not a fusion.
match: [product_id]
scopes: [catalogue]
sources:
  - table: t_products
    map:
      m_product_id: product_id
      m_product_category_id: category_id
      name: product_name
joins:
  - table: t_product_categories   # the lookup: it fuses nothing and adds no row
    from: category_id             # a canonical column of the fused entity
    to: m_product_category_id     # a physical column of the lookup table
    map:
      name: category_name
      description: category_description

The fused entity is compiled exactly as before; the lookups are joined onto it afterwards as a many-to-one LEFT JOIN. For each fused row, the lookup rows whose to column equals the row's from value (see how keys are compared) decide the outcome:

Matching lookup rows The joined columns _conflicts none, or from is empty all empty (NULL) — the product is kept nothing: an absence is not an opinion exactly one that row's values nothing more than one all empty — even when the rows are identical one entry per joined column, listing every duplicate row; a row with no value shows as null ((empty) on screen)

lm view shows lookup ambiguities under Ambiguïtés et divergences, and lm conflicts list lists them with the source conflicts.

docs.title: How join keys are compared
docs.text:
A key is compared as text, except that a plain decimal number is compared by value. The rule reads the value's shape, not the column's type:

These keys match These keys do not 1000021 = 1000021.0 = 1000021.0000 1000021.5 ≠ 1000021.5001 (nothing is rounded) 1.5 = 1.50 01 ≠ 1, 007 ≠ 7 '1' = '1.0', even in a text column C1 ≠ c1 +5, 1E7, more than 38 digits: compared as text

Two lookup rows whose keys are the same number (5 and 5.0000) are one ambiguous key, as in the table above. The search index of a joined column follows the same rule.

A key whose from and to are both dates or times is compared as dates:

from and to Matches on one of them a date (a lookup keyed by day is a calendar) the UTC day: 2026-07-01 14:30 finds the row of 2026-07-01 both times the instant text on either side the rule above, as text

A from whose sources mix dates and times is a time, so it meets a calendar at the day. Matched at the day, a lookup whose to holds times has one key per day: two of its rows on one day are an ambiguous key, as two equal numbers are — the joined columns empty, both rows in _conflicts.

Rules worth knowing:

  • a join is always a many-to-one left join; there is no type:;
  • joins[] is flat and reads only the fused entity's columns, so cycles cannot be declared;
  • joined columns are readable, filterable, askable and exportable like any other; the entity's scopes bound the whole entity;
  • a joined column can be indexed by a kind: SearchIndex; a lookup row that arrives later re-projects the rows holding its key;
  • on a resolution: entity, the joins are read on top of the resolved view.
Apply refusal When 400 from is not a column the sources produce, a joined name collides, or the lookup is also a source 400 naming the lookup table and column to or a map key does not exist in the lookup table 409 run the source connectors first the lookup table does not exist yet

docs.title: Deliver the joined entity to S3
docs.text:
A joined entity exports like any other: its joined columns are canonical columns, so an Export can name them. The demo ships the whole case — two CSV files, the two connectors that ingest them, the Entity above and an export of it:

The manifests read /tmp/acme-catalogue/ on the hub's filesystem; no lm command places a file there, so copy it into the container:

docker exec lumnik-hub-1 mkdir -p /tmp/acme-catalogue
for f in m_product m_product_category; do docker cp docs/apps/demo/data/$f.csv lumnik-hub-1:/tmp/acme-catalogue/; done
lm apply -f docs/apps/demo/sources/40-products.yaml
lm apply -f docs/apps/demo/sources/50-product-categories.yaml
lm connector run products && lm connector run product-categories
# `connector run` answers once the run is accepted, not finished: wait for both to read Completed
lm run list --connector products
lm run list --connector product-categories
lm entity apply -f docs/apps/demo/entities/30-product-with-category.yaml

The join is proven in the terminal, before anything is delivered anywhere:

$ lm entity get ProductWithCategory --filter product_id=P1 -o table
PRODUCT_ID  CATEGORY_ID  PRODUCT_NAME  CATEGORY_NAME  CATEGORY_DESCRIPTION        _CONFLICTS
P1          C1           Pump 50       Pumps          Centrifugal and gear pumps  {}

category_name and category_description come from the category lookup, joined on category_id. The four products:

$ lm entity get ProductWithCategory
PRODUCT_ID  CATEGORY_ID  PRODUCT_NAME  CATEGORY_NAME  CATEGORY_DESCRIPTION        _CONFLICTS
P1          C1           Pump 50       Pumps          Centrifugal and gear pumps  {}
P2          C1           Pump 80       Pumps          Centrifugal and gear pumps  {}
P3          C9           Spare gasket                                             {}
P4          C2           Valve DN15                                               {"category_name": [{"src": "t_product_categories", "value": "Valves"}, {"src": "t_product_categories", "value": "Valves (old)"}], "category_description": [{"src": "t_product_categories", "value": "Ball valves"}, {"src": "t_product_categories", "value": "Superseded listing"}]}

P3 points at a category the lookup does not have; P4 at one it lists twice, so its category cells are empty and the ledger lists both rows.

lm secret set OUTBOUND_S3_ACCESS_KEY      # prompts without echo; the names the export references
lm secret set OUTBOUND_S3_SECRET_KEY
lm export apply -f docs/apps/exports/30-product-catalogue-s3.yaml   # edit bucket and region first
lm export run product-catalogue --wait

# 30-product-catalogue-s3.yaml — the joined entity, delivered to an S3 bucket.
#
# One row per product, the category's name and description alongside. A product whose category
# is unknown, or listed twice, is delivered with those cells empty. For a local MinIO add
# `endpoint: http://minio:9000` under destination.
apiVersion: apps.lumnik.io/v1
kind: Export
metadata:
  name: product-catalogue
spec:
  scope: catalogue
  source:
    entity: ProductWithCategory
  columns: [product_id, product_name, category_id, category_name, category_description]
  order: [product_id]
  format:
    kind: csv
  destination:
    kind: s3
    bucket: acme-outbound
    prefix: catalogue/
    filename: products.csv
    region: eu-west-3
    access_key_env: OUTBOUND_S3_ACCESS_KEY
    secret_key_env: OUTBOUND_S3_SECRET_KEY
  mode: snapshot
  • The object has a header line, then one row per product in product_id order — the four rows above.
  • The run's receipt gives the object's location, row count and SHA-256 of the bytes sent.
  • The export's scope must be one of the entity's.

docs.title: The columns: grounding block
docs.text:
This is where you teach the surfaces what a column means — the input the ask guards enforce and the labels a view renders:

Key Meaning label the human name — a kind: View prints it as the column header and the detail's field name, Recherche shows it on its results; the schema card shows it beside the raw name description the business meaning, fed to the SQL-generation prompt so the model stops guessing example an example value, same purpose values the allowed domain — a filter on any other value is refused, not run (the domain guard) prefer the source table that goes first for this column: each system is the reference for its own fields

A terse question such as status SO-000004 needs an example on the identifier column, or the model abstains: nothing ties that shape to a column. Declare a synthetic one (example: SO-000001); the schema card carries only what you declare.

The rows a question returns are sent to the configured model to phrase the answer — see Models.

After the quickstart's manifest, the scope's card carries the labels:

$ lm source schema --scope desk
…
connector.v_acmecustomer
  code                     text           — Code client
  name                     text           — Raison sociale
  city                     text           — Ville
  segment                  text           — Segment
  credit_limit             text           — Encours autorisé
  email                    text           — Email

and a filter outside the declared domain is refused wherever the entity is read:

$ lm view -f docs/apps/demo/views/10-customers.yaml --filter segment=PLATINUM
Error: API error 400: 'PLATINUM' is not an allowed value for segment (allowed: GOLD, SILVER, BRONZE)

A grounded column must exist in the canonical shape (a typo is refused at apply), and a declared value may not be blank or carry leading or trailing whitespace — it would never exact-match and would silently zero-row:

$ lm entity apply -f docs/apps/demo/entities/64-refused-domain-whitespace.yaml
Error: API error 400: column 'segment' has an allowed value with leading/trailing whitespace (would never exact-match): ' SILVER'

docs.title: Each system for its own fields — prefer
docs.text:
A contract system is the reference for the plan; the member portal, where members type their own move, for the address. One source order cannot say both, so the address names its source:

sources:
  - table: t_member_gestion      # first: wins every column that names no other
    map: { member_no: member_no, plan: plan, street: street, city: city }
  - table: t_member_portail
    map: { member_no: member_no, plan: plan, street: street, city: city, email: email }
columns:
  street: { prefer: t_member_portail }
  city:   { prefer: t_member_portail }
  • The portal's street is shown; the contract system's plan still is.
  • Still first non-null: a member with no street in the portal gets the contract system's.
  • Nothing is hidden: a disagreement stays in _conflicts, the preferred source's value first.
  • Each column on its own: preferring both street and city does not tie them together. If the portal holds a street and no city, the city comes from the next source.
  • Refused at apply: a table that is not one of sources[], a source that does not map the column, a match: column.

docs.title: Askable immediately
docs.text:
If the entity declares scopes, apply rediscovers each scope's schema card for the calling tenant, so the fused view is in the chat's vocabulary at once:

$ lm ask --scope desk "Combien de clients GOLD sont à Lyon, et quel est leur encours autorisé total ?"
Il y a 2 clients GOLD à Lyon et leur encours autorisé total est de 2096.
  data as of: 2026-10-16T08:43:46.474408Z (last completed run)

  disputed — a source disagrees on a value this answer filtered on:
    P-1008  city = 'Lyon'  counted  t_acme_desk_erp: Lyon · t_acme_desk_crm: Villeurbanne

  GOLD_CUSTOMERS_COUNT  TOTAL_CREDIT_LIMIT
  2                     2096
  1 row returned

  SQL: SELECT COUNT(*) AS gold_customers_count, SUM(CAST(credit_limit AS INTEGER)) AS total_credit_limit
FROM connector."v_acmecustomer"
WHERE city = 'Lyon' AND segment = 'GOLD'
LIMIT 500

  try: lm conflicts list  — where this scope has source conflicts or lookup ambiguities, row by row

And when the filter matches nothing, a record the fused view filtered out is named too:

$ lm ask --scope desk "Quels clients sont à Villeurbanne ?"
La requête n'a renvoyé aucune ligne. Il peut n'y en avoir réellement aucune, ou la requête n'a pas saisi votre question — vérifiez le SQL avant d'affirmer qu'il n'y en a pas.
  data as of: 2026-10-16T08:43:46.474408Z (last completed run)

  disputed — a source disagrees on a value this answer filtered on:
    P-1008  city = 'Villeurbanne'  not counted  t_acme_desk_erp: Lyon · t_acme_desk_crm: Villeurbanne

  no rows returned

  SQL: SELECT v.code, v.name, v.city, v.segment, v.credit_limit, v.email
FROM connector."v_acmecustomer" v
WHERE v.city = 'Villeurbanne'
LIMIT 500

  try: lm conflicts list  — where this scope has source conflicts or lookup ambiguities, row by row
  • The model answers in the question's language. The hub's own sentences (the zero-row warning above) follow --lang, else your locale (fr_FR here). The SQL and the lines lm writes (data as of, the table, the row count) stay in English.
  • The card refresh at apply is best-effort: if a scope is missing from the chat, lm source rediscover --scope <tag> rebuilds its card.

docs.title: Refusals
docs.text:
Every refusal is a 400 from apply, quoting the exact problem. The ones an integrator meets first, each pinned by a file under docs/apps/demo/entities/:

$ lm entity apply -f docs/apps/demo/entities/60-refused-no-match-column.yaml
Error: API error 400: source 't_acme_desk_crm' does not map the match column: code
$ lm entity apply -f docs/apps/demo/entities/61-refused-case-collision.yaml
Error: API error 400: canonical column 'email' conflicts with 'Email' across sources (case-insensitive collision); use one consistent case
$ lm entity apply -f docs/apps/demo/entities/62-refused-reserved.yaml
Error: API error 400: source 't_acme_desk_erp': canonical column '_src' is reserved
$ lm entity apply -f docs/apps/demo/entities/65-refused-missing-table.yaml
Error: API error 409: source relation "connector.t_acme_desk_nowhere" does not exist — the entity fuses tables its source connectors create; run the source connectors first, then apply again

The last one is a 409, not a 400: the manifest is fine, the world is not ready for it yet.

Refusal Meaning Fix kind must be 'Entity' wrong or missing kind kind: Entity name must be a simple identifier (letters, digits, _) — it becomes the SQL view name v_<name> advertised to the chat: … the name flows into SQL and the chat rename match must declare at least one column v1 needs one match rule declare the join key match declares a duplicate column (case-insensitive): … the same key listed twice remove the duplicate sources must have at least one source / source '…' map must have at least one column an entity fuses real tables declare table + map source '…': canonical column '…' is reserved the name is one of the reserved names pick another canonical name source '…' maps duplicate canonical column (case-insensitive): … two source columns feeding one canonical column in the same source keep one canonical column '…' conflicts with '…' across sources (case-insensitive collision); use one consistent case email vs Email would silently become two SQL columns one consistent spelling source '…' does not map the match column: … every source must produce the match column, same case — else its rows could never be matched add it to that source's map scope must be lowercase, start with a letter, then letters/digits/_/- (max 41): … a scope is a Keycloak role name — the same rule as connector scopes, see Scopes rename the scope unknown key(s) in the manifest: … a key kind:Entity does not honor — scope: for scopes: the message lists what it honors columns references unknown canonical column '…' (known: …) grounding for a column that does not exist — almost always a typo use a canonical name column '…' has a blank allowed value / … has an allowed value with leading/trailing whitespace … a domain value that can never match makes the guard lie trim or remove it 409 source relation "…" does not exist — … run the source connectors first a sources[].table no connector has created yet run the source connector, then re-apply 400 source table …: column "…" does not exist — check the sources[].map keys … a sources[].map key the physical table does not have: a typo, or a column renamed upstream since the last apply fix the key to the column the connector creates, then re-apply

docs.title: Read API
docs.text:
lm entity get NAME [--filter COLUMN=VALUE]… [--limit N] [--offset N] [-o table|json|yaml]

lm_user. The fused rows, each with its _conflicts ledger ({} when no conflict). The name is case-insensitive; an unknown entity is a 404, an empty result prints no rows.

Option Effect --filter COLUMN=VALUE exact match on a canonical column; repeatable (AND). _conflicts is not filterable --limit N 1..1000, default 100; a full page prints note: result hit the limit on stderr --offset N skip N rows, to page further

A date column reads as its UTC instant, 2026-07-01T00:00:00.000500Z, or as its day, 2026-07-02; --filter due=2026-07-01 is equal as an instant (the day's midnight UTC), as in a view. A number column is equal by value, --filter amount=1500.00 finding 1500. Every other column is text and --filter matches it exactly; a timestamp held as text reads in UTC, 2026-07-01 00:00:00+00, whatever zone the hub runs in.

  • A scope-bound user who holds none of the entity's scopes gets 403 scope not granted (see Scopes).
  • lm refuses a filter named limit, offset or identity, a column named twice, and a filter naming no column (when the page has rows to prove it).
  • For a resolution: entity, the history behind a row is on kind: Entity — resolve.
  • From a script or another system: GET /api/entities/{name}, with ?<column>=value, ?limit=, ?offset=. Over HTTP an unknown parameter is ignored, not refused.

docs.title: Aggregated conflicts
docs.text:
Where do my entities hold a source conflict or a lookup ambiguity, across every entity I may read?

$ lm conflicts list
ENTITY        KEY     COLUMNS  SOURCES
AcmeCustomer  P-1000  name     t_acme_desk_erp,t_acme_desk_crm
AcmeCustomer  P-1002  city     t_acme_desk_erp,t_acme_desk_crm
AcmeCustomer  P-1008  city     t_acme_desk_erp,t_acme_desk_crm

lm_user. One row per record still in dispute, by entity then match key; --limit N (default 100, up to 1000). The TUI's :conflicts page shows the full ledger under d.

  • A resolution: entity's key is the record's entity id, or <source table>:<source id> while nothing has resolved it.
  • A scope-bound user's list omits the entities they hold no scope for, without a 403.
  • An entity whose view is missing or fails when read (5-second timeout) is skipped and logged; the rest of the list still answers.
  • Over HTTP: GET /api/entities/conflicts?limit=N.

docs.title: Remove
docs.text:
$ lm connector delete acme-desk-erp
Error: API error 409: table connector.t_acme_desk_erp feeds entity acmecustomer — remove the entity first (lm entity delete acmecustomer)
$ lm entity delete acmecustomer
Type 'delete' to delete entity acmecustomer — its view, for every tenant: delete
deleted: acmecustomer
$ lm connector delete acme-desk-erp
Error: API error 409: table connector.t_acme_desk_erp feeds entity acmecustomercrmfirst — remove the entity first (lm entity delete acmecustomercrmfirst)
$ lm entity delete acmecustomercrmfirst
Type 'delete' to delete entity acmecustomercrmfirst — its view, for every tenant: delete
deleted: acmecustomercrmfirst
$ lm connector delete acme-desk-erp
Type 'delete' to delete connector acme-desk-erp (csv-file) — 11 rows of connector.t_acme_desk_erp, its run history and RAG chunks: delete
deleted: acme-desk-erp

The 409 names one entity at a time: delete each entity that reads the table, then the connector.

  • lm entity delete (lm_admin) drops the view, the manifest and every search index over the entity, and removes it from its scopes' cards. The prompt names the search indexes when there are some.
  • An entity is declared once for the whole hub: deleting it removes it for every tenant.
  • In a script, pass --force; without it and without a keyboard nothing is deleted: aborted: no confirmation read (EOF) — pass --force in a script.
  • A scope-bound integrator must hold all the entity's scopes. An unknown name is a 404.

docs.title: Fuse two systems' customer tables
docs.text:
lm entity apply -f docs/apps/demo/entities/10-customer.yaml
lm entity get acmecustomer -o json

Result: one canonical row per match key, unioned from every declared source — the first source in sources[] wins a disagreement, and every disagreement is kept in that row's _conflicts ledger.

docs.title: See which source said what, on one record
docs.text:
$ lm view P-1008 -f docs/apps/demo/views/10-customers.yaml
Clients ACME / P-1008

  Code client        P-1008
  Raison sociale     Filtration Lyon 1008
  Ville              Lyon
  Segment            GOLD
  Encours autorisé   1596

  (!) Ambiguïtés et divergences
  Ville   t_acme_desk_erp «Lyon» · t_acme_desk_crm «Villeurbanne»

Result: the record's ledger, rendered under Ambiguïtés et divergences ("ambiguities and divergences"); a record with neither ends with ✓ aucune ambiguïté ni divergence instead. The view is kind: View, one file over the entity.

docs.title: Give the fusion a third opinion
docs.text: Add a third entry to sources[] — a legacy table, a Kafka topic's t_* — mapping the match column and whatever else it knows. Result: columns only that source has appear in the shape; a three-way disagreement lists three entries in the ledger; the source that wins one column has no claim on another.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Gesture 404 on lm entity get NAME (or GET /api/entities/{name}) no entity by that name has been applied (lookup is case-insensitive, so casing is not it) check the name against what apply reported, or apply the manifest 403 {"error":"scope not granted"} on a read you hold none of the entity's scopes ask an integrator to grant one of those scope: roles apply refused 409: source relation … does not exist a sources[].table does not exist yet — that source connector never ran run the source connector, then re-apply lm connector delete refused 409: table … feeds entity … the interlock — the entity still fuses that table lm entity delete <name> first a row you expected is missing from the fusion its match column is NULL in that source — excluded by construction give it a key at the source, or accept that it cannot be matched the wrong system's value shows source order is the priority, per column reorder sources[]; the other value is in _conflicts either way a number is a string ("500") every value reads as a string; the column orders as a number only when every source holds a number type the CSV column with parse-number (its table is created again, as for a date), then lm entity apply — see Numbers across sources ids or amounts sort as text (100 before 12) one source holds the column as text the same: every source must hold a number a date is a string, or two sources "disagree" on the same day one source holds the date as text (a CSV left as written) type that column with parse-date: four steps, its table is created again an entity is missing from lm conflicts list you hold none of its scopes, or its view is gone or fails when read check your grants, or the hub log for "compiled view missing" / "compiled view unreadable" entity applied fine, but chat cannot discuss it no scopes declared add scopes: and re-apply; apply rediscovers the cards for you 403 with an empty body you do not hold the role the command requires (lm_admin for apply and delete, lm_user for reads) no lm command lists your roles: GET /api/bff/v1/me returns them under roles

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Every lumnik word, one breath each, grouped by where it lives on the system map. Each entry links to the page that owns the full story.

docs.title: Ingest — sources into the hub
docs.text:
Hub — the lumnik application itself: the service on :8080 that runs the connectors, serves the API and the PWA, and owns the multi-tenant PostgreSQL its ingested data lands in. Hub and database are two components, not one — the stack starts them side by side. Sources are never written to. Deploy it.

Connector — a declared ingestion unit: CSV, JDBC, or REST — GraphQL and SOAP are request shapes on the same REST engine — plus Kafka for inbound events. Overview.

Manifest / kind: — the YAML you apply. Eight kinds in three families: Connector and Entity (ingestion and fusion); View, App, Process, Workflow and Export (the app ladder); SearchIndex (Search). Each kind has its own command: lm apply -f for a connector, lm <kind> apply -f for the others (lm entity, view, app, process, workflow, export, search). How lumnik works.

Endpoint — one queryable surface inside a connector (a table, a file, a REST resource). A run fans out over the connector's enabled endpoints, and the scheduler, cursor and purge all work per endpoint. CLI.

Run — one execution of one endpoint of a connector: lm connector run over a two-table source writes two run rows, and each names the endpoint it read. Each run keeps its arithmetic in a ledger: records in, records out, records skipped. lm run list.

Conservation invariant — records in = records out + records skipped, on every run, always. A row is never silently lost; it arrives, is skipped with a counted reason, or lands in the DLQ (a declared filter is a counted skip, not a DLQ entry). Seeing what was ingested.

DLQ (dead-letter queue) — where a quarantined row waits, carrying its reason and the offending payload, until you close it: discard, or replayed naming the run that carried the row again. The hub never re-reads a dead letter. lm dlq.

Raw table (t_*) — the dynamic table a csv-file, jdbc-generic or kafka connector creates in schema connector, one per endpoint, stamped with the tenant. The untouched landing zone the rest of the system builds on. The rest-generic engine (so GraphQL and SOAP too) is the exception: its hybrid tables take the name the manifest declares, no t_ prefix — the WOW demo's connector.cust_siebel is one.

Transformer — a per-cell repair applied at ingestion — mojibake, legacy date formats — declared in the manifest, at the door. Transformers.

Hook — a Kotlin script (.kts) running inside the mapping pipeline at dataset, row or cell level, for the cases declarative transformers can't express. Kotlin escape hatch.

Watermark — the incremental mode of the JDBC connector: a declared column whose persisted high-water mark lets the next run fetch only what changed. JDBC.

File source / transport — where a CSV physically lives: local, s3 or sftp. Orthogonal to connector types. CSV & files.

docs.title: Fuse — many sources, one truth
docs.text:
Entity — N legacy sources fused into one canonical, queryable thing (the WOW's Customer). Declared by a kind: Entity manifest. Entities.

_conflicts ledger — where fused sources that disagree stay visible, instead of one value silently winning. lm conflicts list.

docs.title: Ask — questions over your data
docs.text:
Edition note — the Open edition has no chat: lm ask and lm chat find no door on its hub, and no chunks are stored. Which edition am I on?

Analytic mode — the chat translates your question to SQL and runs it read-only over the live hub, fenced by the guards. lm ask, TUI :ask, the PWA chat. The five guards.

Semantic mode — retrieval-only chat: it cites ingested chunks and never generates SQL. HTTP API.

Chunk — the retrieval unit: a slice of ingested data embedded into the vector store, scoped, and citable as a source. Models & providers.

Guard — one of five deterministic checks standing between your question and the answer. Four refuse — with a what-to-do-next — rather than guess; the fifth reframes an empty result instead of letting it become a confident "there are none". The five guards.

Asymmetry of harm — the principle behind the guards: a refusal costs you a retry; a confident wrong answer — especially a confident "there are none" — costs you a business decision. Ask honesty.

docs.title: Act — the app ladder
docs.text:
View (kind: View) — a saved, server-side description of what a métier sees: a table, its columns, filters. The PWA and lm discover views from the hub — writes are curated, reads are scope-bound. Views.

App (kind: App) — a métier application's own identity, declared instead of compiled: its title, the scope it reads through, one identifier from the curated icon set, and its accent/background theme. Applied with lm app apply and discovered by the PWA at login. At most one app carries the default flag — the one a bare /app/ opens; once set, it can only be moved to another app. The métier PWA.

Process (kind: Process) — a declarative reaction: when data matching a condition arrives, notify. Refusable by design, like everything on the ladder. Processes.

Workflow (kind: Workflow) — a declared document lifecycle over a status column: states, aliases for dirty legacy spellings, transitions. The chat answers lifecycle questions from the declared graph instead of inventing one. Workflows.

Alias — a dirty-data spelling (en cours, encours) declared to resolve to one canonical state code. Workflows.

Data-truth report — what workflow apply prints: the values found in the data but never declared, and the codes declared but never observed. Workflows.

Dormancy — a watched lifecycle's memory: a non-terminal document observed unmoved past the declared threshold raises a decision.dormant.<workflow> alert. Dormancy.

Inbox — where alerts and decisions surface for a human to see and acknowledge. Inbox.

Outputs / deliveries — the journal of what the hub sent out (webhooks) and whether it arrived — failures first, replayable. lm outputs list.

PWA — the métier app served at /app/: installable on a phone, scope-bound, discovering its views from the hub. The métier PWA.

docs.title: Operate — the integrator's side
docs.text:
lm — the integrator's CLI and TUI, one binary. Every hub surface — connectors, runs, DLQ, ask, views, workflows — has its counterpart there. CLI & TUI reference.

Integrator — the person who wields lm: applies manifests, runs connectors, manages scopes. Role lm_integrator; métier users carry lm_user. Roles & permissions.

TLS façade — the optional Caddy overlay putting hub, PWA and Keycloak behind one https origin — one issuer for every device. Deploy.

docs.title: Security & tenancy
docs.text:
Tenant — one customer space. Isolation lives in the database, not in the URL: every query is filtered by the tenant the connection declares. RLS & database roles.

RLS (Row-Level Security) — the PostgreSQL mechanism enforcing that filter on every row of every tenant-stamped table. RLS & database roles.

Métier — the trade a scope serves — magasinier, comptable — and the register the whole product speaks: per-métier chat, per-métier apps.

Scope — an opt-in boundary inside a tenant, carried as Keycloak roles (scope:<tag>). No scope roles = tenant-wide access; one or more = bound to exactly those. The uniform refusal is 403 {"error":"scope not granted"}. Scopes.

docs.title: How lumnik works
docs.text:
Everything you configure is a YAML manifest. Apply it, then see it in lm or the TUI. Every apply is checked first: refused with the exact field named, or saved.

This page covers what happens when you apply. What happens when a row changes is How lumnik breathes.

docs.title: The kubectl parallel
docs.text:
If you know kubectl, you know most of lm:

  • declarative objects and an idempotent apply -f;
  • a dry run for connectors: lm validate -f;
  • a schema reference for connector types: lm describe connector-type <type>;
  • contexts for several hubs: lm config use-context.

For the other kinds, the fields are on each kind's page, and the TUI's :new opens a valid example of the kind you pick in $EDITOR.

lm apply never reconciles. Apply once and it stays applied until you apply again; nothing pulls the hub or your sources back toward the manifest. The one watcher is a Workflow's dormancy sweep: it raises an alert, and never changes the manifest or the data.

docs.title: Eight kinds, three families
docs.text:
kind: apiVersion: What it declares Apply Owning page Connector connectors.lumnik.io/v1 — required ingestion from one source lm apply -f Connectors Entity none one thing fused from N sources lm entity apply -f Entities View apps.lumnik.io/v1 — not checked a read-only list a métier sees lm view apply -f Views App apps.lumnik.io/v1 — not checked a métier app's title, scope, icon and theme lm app apply -f The métier PWA Process apps.lumnik.io/v1 — not checked a reaction to a row landing lm process apply -f Processes Workflow apps.lumnik.io/v1 — not checked a document lifecycle over a status column lm workflow apply -f Workflows Export apps.lumnik.io/v1 — required a managed delivery of an entity's rows lm export apply -f Exports SearchIndex search.lumnik.io/v1 — required which entity columns an optional Search provider indexes lm search apply -f Choosing what your hub offers
  • Ingest and fuse: Connector, Entity.
  • Apps: View, App, Process, Workflow, Export.
  • Search: SearchIndex.

Connector is the only kind applied with the bare lm apply -f; every other kind has its own prefixed apply.

docs.title: Living with your objects
docs.text:
Kind List Read one Remove Also Connector lm connector list lm connector get NAME (stored fields) lm connector delete NAME run, pause, resume, scope Entity lm entity list lm entity get NAME (rows) lm entity delete NAME export, resolve, ambiguous View lm view list lm view get NAME (manifest) lm view rm NAME lm view NAME renders it App lm app list lm app get NAME (manifest) lm app rm NAME Process lm process list — lm process rm NAME enable, disable Workflow lm workflow list lm workflow get NAME (manifest) lm workflow rm NAME enable, disable Export lm export list lm export get NAME (manifest) — run, runs, status, retry SearchIndex lm search status lm search status NAME lm search rm NAME query, rebuild, cancel
  • An Export cannot be removed. Re-applying it without spec.schedule lifts its schedule.
  • No single command lists every kind; each kind keeps its own list.

Full command tables: CLI & TUI reference.

docs.title: One lifecycle
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  write["write the YAML"] --> validate["lm validate<br/>(dry run)"]
  validate --> apply["lm apply<br/>(idempotent)"]
  apply --> observe["observe in the TUI"]
  validate -. refused .-> write
  apply -. refused .-> write

Write, apply, observe — every kind. A refusal at either check sends you back to the file.

Keep manifests in your repository and version them there. If a local file is lost, lm view get, lm app get, lm workflow get and lm export get print the stored manifest back.

docs.title: The little languages inside the YAML
docs.text:
A manifest's fields are plain YAML, but several of them hold a small syntax of their own. Each one is documented in full on the page that owns it — this table is the map, not the manual.

Language One-line syntax note Where it shows up JSONPath $ is the response root — $.data[-1:].id reads "the id of the last element of data" REST/GraphQL/SOAP pagination + promote fields — REST cron 5 fields (UNIX crontab dialect), evaluated in UTC by the hub's own scheduler — no OS cron involved any connector's spec.schedule — Connectors Overview glob * and ? only, in the final filename segment — no ** recursion CSV local/sftp/s3 transport.path — CSV & files date patterns dd/MM/yyyy — capital MM is month, lowercase mm is minutes; add H/h/m/s only when the value carries a time parse-date — Transformers regex full-match vs find semantics — differs per hook regex-extract / regex-replace / filter-where — Transformers {{secret:NAME}} / {{env:NAME}} secret: reads the lm secret registry, then the hub's process environment (OS env var, JVM system property as dev/test fallback); env: reads the environment only; unresolved fails the run fast SOAP body/header templates — SOAP ${now} resolves once, to the ingestion instant enrich-context — Transformers Kotlin .kts the escape hatch — full JVM trust, no sandbox/timeout/memory cap, classpath-only scripts mapping hooks (Transformers) and platform lifecycle/action hooks (developer SPI, documented beside the code)

docs.title: Refusability as a feature
docs.text:
Every apply runs the same checks as validate. A refusal names the field and the fix:

$ lm validate -f acme-nightly.yaml
✗ acme-nightly.yaml — 1 error(s), 0 warning(s)

  ERROR    spec.archive_path
          archive_path is required when after_process=move
          → Set archive_path: /path/to/archive/

Fix errors above before running 'lm apply -f acme-nightly.yaml'.
Error: validation failed: 1 error(s)

More refusals and warnings: Connectors — Validate before apply.

docs.text:

  • Views · Apps · Processes · Workflows · Exports — the app kinds.

docs.title: Integration as code
docs.text:
An integrator who defrosts one ERP writes its universe once: a directory of YAML manifests, one per connector, entity, view, app, process and workflow. That directory is the installation. It goes in git, it is reviewed in a pull request, and it is replayed against another tenant by a loop.

This page is the operating manual for that. Four habits of lm make the loop possible:

  • a manifest arrives through -f, and -f - reads it from stdin;
  • listings print -o json|yaml;
  • notes and warnings go to stderr, so stdout stays parseable;
  • the exit code carries the verdict.

docs.title: What belongs in the repository
docs.text:
In git Never in git Rebuilt, not stored kind: Connector, Entity, View, App, Process, Workflow, Export, SearchIndex manifests secret values — manifests carry the name (password_env, token_env, key_env), never the credential the dynamic tables under schema connector (ingestion writes them) hook scripts (META-INF/hooks.yaml, deployed with the extension — not applied through lm) the OIDC token in ~/.lm/config.yaml the RAG corpus (re-indexed from what was ingested) the apply order (below) — a Makefile or a numbered prefix ingested rows, dead letters, run history discovered schema cards (lm source rediscover)

Credentials are referenced by name and resolved where the hub runs — its environment or its secret store, depending on the connector; each connector page states which. A manifest is therefore safe to commit, and the same manifest works against dev, staging and production because only the name travels.

Two fields break that, and a repository should ban them

Two manifest fields take a secret inline, both declared dev/test only:

Field Kind What it does spec.connection.password jdbc-generic Wins over password_env when both are present — a manifest that looks safe because it names an env var is still overridden by the plain-text line above it. spec.auth.token_value rest-generic A literal bearer token. token_env is read first, so nothing is overridden — but the secret itself is in the file.

lm validate and lm apply name both — WARN spec.connection.password, WARN spec.auth.token_value — but a warning exits 0, so it gates nothing. Close them in CI, before the validator runs:

! grep -rnE '^[[:space:]]*(password|token_value):' 10-connectors/

acme-si/
├── 10-connectors/      # applied first — an entity fuses sources that must exist
│   ├── ad-user.yaml
│   └── c-order.yaml
├── 20-entities/
│   └── customer.yaml
├── 30-apps/            # views, processes, workflows — they read entities
│   ├── clients-view.yaml
│   └── commande-workflow.yaml
└── secrets.list        # the NAMES the manifests reference, so an operator can check them

Order matters in one direction only: a manifest that references something applies after it. Connectors, then entities, then the app ladder. Within a layer, order is free.

docs.title: The three gestures
docs.text:
lm validate -f 10-connectors/ad-user.yaml   # dry run, per-field errors, exit 1 on error
lm apply    -f 10-connectors/ad-user.yaml   # upsert by metadata.name
lm run list --connector ad_user -o json     # verify: the ledger, as data

apply is an upsert: replaying the whole directory converges a tenant. There is no separate "create" and "update":

$ lm apply -f docs/apps/demo/sources/10-erp.yaml
{"name":"acme-desk-erp","connectorId":"6c8d0ce5-8686-493d-a05d-bdc950281707","endpointsApplied":1}

lm validate covers kind: Connector only

Any other kind fails on the envelope (kind must be "Connector"). The other kinds are checked at apply, which refuses rather than half-writes. A CI gate routes by kind: validate the connectors, apply the rest against a non-production tenant.

docs.title: The pipe, both ways
docs.text:
lm reads manifests from stdin and writes results as data:

  • In — -f - reads the manifest from stdin, at every -f door (apply, validate, entity apply, view apply, app apply, process apply, workflow apply, export apply, search apply, connector apply).
  • Out — -o json (or yaml) on every listing, plus the two discovery surfaces a generator reads: lm source schema and lm source jdbc list-tables. Notes such as "result hit the limit" go to stderr.
  • lm connector scope ls has no -o: it prints one scope per line, ready to pipe.

That pair turns two hundred tables into a loop: lm source schema hands back the tables and columns as data, a generator turns each into a manifest, -f - applies it:

lm source schema --scope atelier -o json \
  | jq -r '.tables[].name' \
  | while read -r table; do
      ./generate-entity.sh "$table" | lm entity apply -f -
    done

On the demo desk:

$ lm source schema --scope desk -o json | jq -c '.tables[] | {name, cols: [.columns[].name]}'
{"name":"connector.t_acme_desk_erp","cols":["code","name","city","segment","credit_limit"]}
{"name":"connector.t_acme_desk_crm","cols":["customer","company","town","email"]}
{"name":"connector.t_acme_desk_orders","cols":["order_no","code","status","amount","ordered_on"]}
{"name":"connector.v_acmecustomer","cols":["code","name","city","segment","credit_limit","email"]}

The generator is yours: it holds your knowledge of that ERP.

The two ends also meet directly. lm view get writes the saved view's manifest to stdout, so promoting a view from one environment to another is one line with no file in between:

lm view get clients --context staging | lm view apply -f - --context prod

Do not do the same with lm connector get | lm connector apply: the flat fields carry the connector's id, which belongs to the tenant it came from. Use the kind: Connector manifest in your repository instead.

A manifest piped in has no file name: refusals name it stdin and point upstream.

$ cat bad-connector.yaml | lm validate -f -
✗ stdin — 2 error(s), 1 warning(s)

  ERROR    spec.transport
          required field missing

  ERROR    spec.after_process
          required field missing
          → archive
          → delete
          → move
          → none

  WARN     metadata.scopes
          no scopes declared — the connector's tables will not be askable in any métier
          → Add: scopes: [compta]  (the métier a user must hold as scope:compta)

Fix the errors above in what produced this manifest.
Error: validation failed: 2 error(s)
$ echo $?
1

docs.title: In CI
docs.text:
lm validate exits 1 when the manifest carries at least one error, 0 otherwise — so it is a gate with no wrapper:

# .github/workflows/manifests.yml
- name: Validate every connector manifest
  env:
    LUMNIK_URL: ${{ secrets.LUMNIK_STAGING_URL }}
    LUMNIK_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.LUMNIK_STAGING_TOKEN }}
  run: |
    for f in 10-connectors/*.yaml; do
      lm validate -f "$f"
    done

# on merge — converge the tenant, then wait for the ledger to settle
- run: |
    for f in 10-connectors/*.yaml 20-entities/*.yaml 30-apps/*.yaml; do lm apply -f "$f"; done
    lm connector run ad_user
    for _ in $(seq 1 60); do
      status=$(lm run list --connector ad_user -o json | jq -r '.[0].status')
      case "$status" in
        Completed|Partial) echo "run ended: $status"; break ;;
        Failed|Cancelled)  echo "run ended: $status"; exit 1 ;;
      esac
      sleep 5
    done

The wait is not optional. lm connector run exits 0 as soon as the run is scheduled:

$ lm connector run acme-desk-erp
run scheduled: 2cff18e6-6774-44f5-bcad-e3640e776f51

Asserting on the ledger at once would read Queued or Running. Runs are listed newest first, so .[0] is the one just scheduled.

Statuses are Queued, Running, Completed, Partial, Failed, Cancelled. Decide whether Partial fails your pipeline: the run read less than its target, nothing broke.

A pre-flight worth one line — the secrets the manifests reference must exist on the target, and secret list never returns a value:

lm secret list -o json | jq -r '.[].name' | sort > present.txt
comm -23 <(sort secrets.list) present.txt   # prints what is missing, empty means ready

Validation is server-side — CI needs a reachable hub

lm validate posts the manifest to the hub; there is no offline validator. A PR gate needs a URL and a token for a non-production tenant. Air-gapped CI can only lint the YAML.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
Command 0 1 lm validate no error (warnings still exit 0) at least one error lm apply and every … apply the manifest was applied rejected, unreachable, unauthorised lm connector run the run was scheduled (run scheduled: <id>, one line per endpoint) it could not be scheduled any command — any error, printed as Error: … on stderr

lm connector run returning 0 means the run was accepted, not that it started. The verdict is in the ledger: wait on lm run list -o json, as above.

docs.title: What a green pipeline does not prove
docs.text:
• Secrets are not in git, so a fresh tenant has none until an operator sets them.
  • Data is not in git. Applying the universe creates the pipes; the rows arrive when the connectors run.
  • Scope roles live in the identity provider (scope:<tag> realm roles), not in a manifest — see Tenants, users & scopes.
  • The ERP is untouched by lumnik either way. Ingestion is read-only: nothing in this repository makes lumnik write to the source system.
  • A replay switches the outputs back on. A kind: Process is enabled when applied and fires at once: webhooks and mail leave the platform. Apply the app layer to a fresh tenant with that in mind, or run lm process disable NAME right after the apply.

Reversing all of it is its own page: Reversibility & exit.

docs.title: Outputs — the roads out
docs.text:
How to wire what leaves the hub: a webhook to n8n or Teams, a mail, a pull. Why and when: How lumnik breathes. In lm ui: :integrations, :notify and :outputs (the terminal console).

Command Roles needed lm integration, lm outputs lm_integrator and lm_admin lm notify lm_admin lm inbox lm_user 
$ lm integration list          # as a user holding lm_admin but not lm_integrator
Error: API error 403: missing role lm_integrator

Wiring is tenant-wide: a webhook or an email rule receives every matching event of the tenant. An admin holding any scope:* role is refused lm integration, lm notify, lm outputs and the live event stream with 403 {"error":"scope not granted"}.

docs.title: The three roads out
docs.text: Road Carries Command family Webhook every subscribed event, signed, retried, journaled, replayable lm integration Email events matching a rule, one mail per event, best-effort lm notify Pull the decision pile and the delivery journal, when you come asking lm inbox · lm outputs

docs.title: Wire a webhook
docs.text:
echo -n "$SIGNING_SECRET" | lm integration add crm-bridge \
  --url https://n8n.example.com/webhook/lumnik \
  --events 'decision.*' \
  --secret-stdin
lm integration test <ID>          # fires a real POST at the target, result inline
  • --events takes exact types or a prefix ending in .* (default decision.*). The registry below is the vocabulary.
  • The signing secret rides stdin, never argv — it is stored encrypted and never returned by list/describe.
  • test fires a catalog event (--event, default org.created); decision.* types are dynamic and not testable this way — trigger the rule instead.
  • Forwarding starts at registration — nothing is delivered retroactively.
  • Without --secret-stdin the hub refuses the registration (400) and stores nothing.
  • list and describe show the target's scheme and host only: a webhook URL's path and query are often its credential. -o json / -o yaml print the hub's body as it is, full URL included — that is the machine contract, and you asked for it.
$ echo -n "$SIGNING_SECRET" | lm integration add n8n \
    --url https://n8n.example.com/webhook/lumnik --events 'decision.*' --secret-stdin
registered: n8n (id 1001) — forwards subscribed events from now on
$ lm integration list
ID    NAME  URL                      EVENTS      ENABLED
1001  n8n   https://n8n.example.com  decision.*  true

docs.title: What arrives, and how to verify it
docs.text:
One HTTP POST per event, JSON payload as in the registry, with three headers:

X-Lumnik-Event: decision.commande-bloquee
X-Lumnik-Event-Id: 3639
X-Lumnik-Signature: sha256=<hex HMAC-SHA256 of the raw request body, keyed with your secret>
  • Verify: recompute the HMAC over the raw body bytes and compare; reject on mismatch. n8n and Make have HMAC-verification nodes — give them the value after sha256=.
  • X-Lumnik-Event-Id is the id lm inbox shows, and the decision_id a later annotation.decision.acked carries. A replay keeps it. It is not signed.

docs.title: Delivery semantics
docs.text:
The outbox is swept every 5 s; a failed delivery is retried by a 30 s sweep, 3 attempts in total, per target — a target that already succeeded is not sent the event again. Delivery is at-least-once: a hub stop mid-send can deliver an event twice, so deduplicate on X-Lumnik-Event-Id.

Every attempt lands in the journal:

lm outputs list                   # deliveries across every integration, failures first
lm integration describe <ID>      # one target's registration; :integrations adds its recent deliveries

A decision fired while the target was down — the journal says so, failures first:

$ lm outputs list
ID  INTEGRATION     EVENT                   STATUS       WHEN              ERROR
41  ops-automation  decision.order-on-hold  no response  2026-09-05 05:40  ConnectException: null
A delivery that exhausted its attempts can be replayed: lm outputs replay ID (or ^R on :outputs in lm ui).

What Kept Setting Purged delivery journal (payload + receiver's response) 90 days; 0 = forever LUMNIK_WEBHOOKS_DELIVERY_RETENTION_DAYS daily, 05:00 — a purged delivery cannot be replayed; one still being retried is kept events (the outbox) 30 days LUMNIK_EVENTS_RETENTION_DAYS daily, 04:30 — never past what the slowest consumer has read

docs.title: Route events to email
docs.text:
$ lm notify add --events 'decision.*' --to adv@example.com --template decision-alert
rule 1000: decision.* → adv@example.com
$ lm notify list
ID    EVENTS      RECIPIENT        TEMPLATE        ENABLED
1000  decision.*  adv@example.com  decision-alert  true

One mail per matching event, rendered through a template that can reach into the payload — see Email notifications. Mocked until the SMTP knobs are set; a failed send is not retried — when delivery must be provable, use the webhook.

docs.title: Wire n8n in two minutes
docs.text:
In n8n, add a Webhook node and copy its production URL. Then:

echo -n "$SIGNING_SECRET" | lm integration add n8n \
  --url https://n8n.example.com/webhook/lumnik --events 'decision.*' --secret-stdin
lm integration test <ID>

Result: the test fires a real org.created POST — the n8n execution list shows it within seconds, with X-Lumnik-Event and the sha256= signature ready for an HMAC node.

docs.title: Replay a delivery that exhausted its attempts
docs.text:
lm outputs list                       # failures first — the ID column
lm outputs replay <ID>

Result: one fresh attempt at the same target with the same payload; the outcome lands in the journal like any delivery.

docs.title: Nothing arrives — the four checks
docs.text:
1. Registered after the event? Forwarding starts at registration — nothing is retroactive. Trigger the event again.
  2. Watching data.row.changed on a REST/GraphQL/SOAP-ingested table? Those tables emit no events (named limits).
  3. Was anything subscribed at ingest time? data.row.changed is only emitted when a subscription exists when the row lands — wire first, then re-run the ingestion.
  4. Is it the pipe or the event? lm integration test <ID> proves the pipe; lm outputs list gives the journal's verdict on every real attempt.

docs.title: The event registry
docs.text:
The hub's governed vocabulary — what --events patterns match against and what each payload carries. decision.<name> types are dynamic: your kind: Process rules and dormancy watches mint them under the enforced decision. prefix.

Every event type, from the registry the hub ships (events.yaml) 
module: core
version: "0.1"
events:
  - type: org.created
    description: "A new organisation was created."
    payload:
      orgId: long
      tenantId: long
      name: string
  - type: org.updated
    description: "An organisation was updated."
    payload:
      orgId: long
      tenantId: long
  - type: org.moved
    description: "An organisation's parent changed."
    payload:
      orgId: long
      tenantId: long
      newParentId: long
  - type: org.archived
    description: "An organisation was archived."
    payload:
      id:   long
      code: string
  - type: connector.run.started
    description: "A connector endpoint run started."
    payload:
      run_id:       string
      connector_id: string
      endpoint_id:  string
      sync_mode:    string
      trigger:      string
  - type: connector.run.completed
    description: "A connector endpoint run completed; carries the conservation counters."
    payload:
      run_id:      string
      endpoint_id: string
      records_in:  long
      records_out: long
      duration_ms: long
      tables:      map
  - type: connector.run.partial
    description: "A connector endpoint run ended below the target it gave itself: it wrote everything it read, and did not read everything there was."
    payload:
      run_id:        string
      endpoint_id:   string
      records_in:    long
      records_out:   long
      duration_ms:   long
      tables:        map
      error_message: string
  - type: connector.run.cancelled
    description: "A connector endpoint run was cancelled."
    payload:
      run_id: string
  - type: connector.run.failed
    description: "A connector endpoint run failed."
    payload:
      run_id:        string
      error_message: string
      retryable:     boolean
  - type: platform.secret.created
    description: "A platform secret was created."
    payload:
      name: string
      by:   string
      at:   string
  - type: platform.secret.updated
    description: "A platform secret's value was rotated."
    payload:
      name:              string
      by:                string
      at:                string
      previousRotatedAt: string
  - type: platform.secret.deleted
    description: "A platform secret was deleted."
    payload:
      name: string
      by:   string
      at:   string
  - type: platform.secret.read
    description: "A platform secret was read from the database (cache misses only)."
    payload:
      name: string
      by:   string
      at:   string
  - type: data.row.changed
    description: "A genuinely new or changed row landed in a watched ingest table; emitted in the ingestion transaction."
    payload:
      entity:     string
      entity_key: string
      op:         string
      run_id:     string
  - type: annotation.decision.acked
    description: "A human treated a decision in the inbox."
    payload:
      decision_id: long
      by:          string

Two emission rules worth planning around:

  • data.row.changed is emitted only when an integration, rule or process subscribes to it, and only for jdbc, CSV and kafka ingestion (named limits).
  • decision.* is the métier layer: minted by Processes and Workflow dormancy, treated in the Inbox — annotation.decision.acked closes the loop with who and when.

docs.text:
